The nineteen-thirty-nine New York World's Fair, held in Flushing Meadows in Queens, was a celebration of progress and technological optimism that existed amid the dark shadows of economic depression and impending global conflict. Its ambitious theme, "Building the World of Tomorrow," offered escapism and hope during the Great Depression and amid the geopolitical tensions that were building in Europe. Over forty-four million visitors came to explore its exhibits and attractions. The fair's iconic symbols were the Trylon, a triangular obelisk, and the Perisphere, a colossal sphere, architectural symbols that became emblematic of nineteen-thirties futurism and optimism about humanity's future. These structures dominated the fairgrounds and captured the imagination of visitors. The fair included the Futurama exhibit, a remarkable envisioning designed by industrial designer Norman Bel Geddes. It showed an imagined automated city of the future with elevated highways and integrated urban planning systems that seemed fantastical to contemporary observers. The fair displayed cutting-edge technology of the era, including early television demonstrations that many people had never seen before, advanced automobiles representing the future of transportation, and household innovations that promised to transform domestic life. The exposition was held on twelve hundred sixteen acres in Flushing Meadows, a former wasteland that had been transformed by planner Robert Moses into fair infrastructure. After the fair, this land became permanent parkland. Despite opening just months before World War II began, the fair symbolised pre-war American confidence and aspirations to shape modernity for the century to come.
